stem: A long-running research agent on the Messages API makes dozens of fetch and file-read tool calls per session. To stay under its context limit, the team enabled server-side tool result clearing with a low trigger threshold. Context now stays small, but per-session input cost rose and cache reads dropped sharply: clearing fires on almost every turn and removes only a few thousand tokens each time. Which change best fixes the cost regression while keeping tool result clearing?

options.text: Disable prompt caching for these sessions, since tool result clearing makes cached prefixes stale and the cache writes are wasted on every turn.
Move the clearing into the application so it edits its own history before each request, leaving the prefix the API caches unchanged.
Require each clearing pass to remove a substantial minimum of tokens with clear_at_least, so the cache invalidation is paid rarely and amortized.
Switch to thinking block clearing instead, since clearing thinking blocks frees comparable context while leaving the prompt cache intact.

explanation: Tool result clearing invalidates the cached prompt prefix whenever content is cleared, so each clearing pass incurs a fresh cache write. Clearing a few thousand tokens nearly every turn pays that write repeatedly for little context gained. The documented remedy is to clear enough tokens per pass to make the invalidation worthwhile, which the clear_at_least parameter enforces; later requests then reuse the newly cached prefix.

distractorNotes.a: Plausible because clearing does invalidate the cache, but abandoning caching removes the read savings entirely; the documented fix is to clear less often in larger amounts.
distractorNotes.b: Editing earlier turns client-side still changes the prompt prefix the API sees, so it invalidates the cache just the same, and it gives up the server-side mechanism.
distractorNotes.d: Thinking block clearing preserves the cache only while thinking blocks are kept; clearing them invalidates the cache at that point, and it does not target tool results.

sourceNote: Context editing and prompt caching: tool result clearing invalidates cached prefixes; use clear_at_least

stem: An enterprise security agent analyzes external code contributions submitted to open-source repositories. The agent must inspect untrusted pull request patches, query public package registries, and run static analysis tools. Security policy dictates that untrusted code strings or malicious instructions embedded in pull request comments must not be able to execute unauthorized shell commands or modify local files in the root execution environment. Which orchestration pattern best enforces this boundary?

options.text: Delegate untrusted code and comment inspection to a specialized read-only subagent with an isolated context window and restricted tool permissions, returning only structured diagnostic findings to the primary agent.

Execute all inspection tasks within the primary agent session while appending a persistent system prompt instruction directing Claude to disregard any instructions contained within retrieved pull request comments or commits.

Employ peer-to-peer message passing across multiple autonomous worker agents that share a single underlying shell environment, using an external post-processing filter to intercept disallowed bash commands after execution.
Implement an Evaluator-Optimizer loop where a primary agent executes shell tools and a secondary evaluator agent inspects command outputs afterward to detect whether an exploit was executed.

explanation: Subagents execute in isolated context windows with their own scoped tool sets and system prompts. Delegating the ingestion of untrusted inputs to a child agent configured with read-only tools prevents prompt injection payloads from accessing sensitive write or execution tools. The child agent returns only vetted, structured text findings to the orchestrator, neutralizing injection attempts. Relying on system prompt instructions, post-execution command inspection, or shared execution environments fails to establish a secure privilege boundary.

distractorNotes.b: Prompt-level instructions to ignore malicious comments cannot guarantee security against adversarial prompt injections when untrusted data shares the execution context with privileged tools.
distractorNotes.c: Sharing an underlying shell environment breaks isolation; if any peer agent is subverted by untrusted input, the shared environment and credentials are fully compromised.
distractorNotes.d: An Evaluator-Optimizer loop that inspects actions after execution is a reactive detection mechanism rather than an execution boundary; the exploit has already executed.

sourceNote: Subagents provide context and tool isolation; restrict tools to read-only for untrusted inputs

stem: An order fulfillment platform automates customer cancellation requests requiring coordination across inventory reservation, payment processing, and notification services. The team initially deployed a decentralized peer-to-peer agent architecture where each domain agent directly invoked the next agent. In production, transient payment gateway timeouts cause tasks to stall, fail silently, or initiate circular handoffs. Which architectural refactoring best restores reliable end-to-end execution?

options.text: Retain the peer-to-peer delegation graph but increase the maximum conversation turn limit on each agent, allowing stalled agents additional retries before abandoning their handoffs.
Transition to an orchestrator-workers pattern where a central orchestrator dynamically decomposes the request, delegates scoped subtasks to specialist workers, and synthesizes the results.
Replace the specialist domain agents with a single monolithic prompt that receives all customer cancellation inputs and performs all service updates sequentially within a single conversation turn.
Have peer agents publish intermediate cancellation state to an uncoordinated shared message bus, relying on individual subscribers to determine when an order is finalized.

explanation: In 'Building Effective Agents', Anthropic defines the orchestrator-workers pattern where a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them to worker LLMs, and synthesizes their results. Decentralized or ad-hoc chaining across independent workers lacks centralized coordination to break down dynamic dependencies and synthesize outcomes, leading to fragmented state and stalled handoffs. An orchestrator coordinates subtask dispatch and synthesizes worker outputs into a cohesive result.

distractorNotes.a: Increasing turn limits does not resolve circular delegation or state fragmentation, and it can prolong latency or consume excessive tokens when handoffs stall.
distractorNotes.c: A single monolithic prompt combines unrelated tool schemas and business logic into one context window, increasing error rates and losing modular domain isolation.
distractorNotes.d: An uncoordinated shared message bus lacks a centralized coordinator to handle transaction rollbacks, timeout escalation, or authoritative state reconciliation.

sourceNote: Orchestrator-workers: a central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates to worker LLMs, and synthesizes results

stem: An automated site reliability engineering agent responds to high-severity infrastructure alerts. The agent must gather diagnostics from distributed tracing backends, server logs, and metrics stores before synthesizing a mitigation plan. To minimize time-to-mitigation and avoid degrading model reasoning, the architecture must parallelize data collection while keeping raw telemetry dumps out of the primary reasoning loop. Which TWO design practices best achieve these goals? (Select TWO)

options.text: Deploy specialized diagnostic collector subagents concurrently to query their respective observability backends in parallel.
Chain diagnostic collectors sequentially in a prompt chain so that each collector appends its complete raw payload to the next query.
Require each diagnostic subagent to filter raw telemetry and return only concise, structured diagnostic summaries to the orchestrator.
Execute all telemetry queries within the primary orchestrator session using standard bash tools so all agents share active context.
Stream raw log entries directly into the orchestrator system prompt using dynamic variables updated at high frequency during analysis.

explanation: Running specialized subagents in parallel (fan-out) minimizes data collection latency by querying independent telemetry stores concurrently rather than serially. Furthermore, requiring subagents to analyze raw logs and metrics within their own isolated context windows and return only concise, structured summaries protects the orchestrator from context pollution and token bloat. Chaining collectors sequentially increases latency, running queries in the main session floods the context window with raw text, and streaming raw logs into the system prompt busts prompt caching.

distractorNotes.b: Sequential chaining introduces unnecessary serial latency and forces downstream collectors to carry growing volumes of raw, unparsed telemetry.
distractorNotes.d: Running queries in the root session dumps high-volume raw telemetry into the primary context window, consuming token budget and degrading reasoning performance.
distractorNotes.e: Injecting high-frequency dynamic log data into the system prompt invalidates prompt cache prefixes on every turn and rapidly exceeds token limits.

sourceNote: Subagents parallelize execution and isolate large raw outputs from the orchestrator context

stem: A code modernization platform automates the extraction of legacy monolithic applications into modular packages. Because codebases vary widely, the number of target packages, shared library dependencies, and interface boundaries cannot be predicted before analyzing the abstract syntax tree. The team needs an architecture where an initial analysis determines the required work packages, delegates scoped refactoring tasks to concurrent workers, and merges their outputs. Which workflow pattern best fits this requirement?

options.text: Static sectioning parallelization where a predetermined number of worker prompts process hardcoded subdirectories independently.
An Evaluator-Optimizer loop that prompts a single model to rewrite the entire repository repeatedly until all unit tests pass cleanly.
A fixed prompt chain that passes the entire codebase sequentially through extraction, dependency resolution, and test generation steps.
An Orchestrator-Workers architecture where a lead agent analyzes the code dynamically, spawns modular subtasks, and reconciles results.

explanation: The Orchestrator-Workers pattern is explicitly designed for complex tasks where the required subtasks cannot be predicted in advance. A central orchestrator examines the input dynamically, determines how many worker subtasks are needed and what their scopes should be, delegates the work to specialist workers, and synthesizes their results into a cohesive output. Static sectioning and fixed prompt chains require pre-known task boundaries, while an unsegmented Evaluator-Optimizer loop on a full repository quickly exceeds context capacity.

distractorNotes.a: Static sectioning relies on predetermined task boundaries, which fails when package boundaries depend on dynamic syntax tree analysis.
distractorNotes.b: Rewriting an entire monolithic repository in a single prompt loop exceeds context and output limits and lacks targeted modular decomposition.
distractorNotes.c: A fixed prompt chain cannot dynamically adapt its decomposition when different modules require differing numbers of extraction steps.

sourceNote: Orchestrator-workers dynamically decomposes tasks when subtasks cannot be predicted in advance

stem: In an automated bug-fixing system based on the orchestrator-workers pattern, a lead agent delegates two concurrent tasks on a repository: Worker 1 optimizes database connection pooling in src/db.py, while Worker 2 refactors error handling across the same file. Both workers complete their tasks successfully and return valid unified diffs. However, when the system applies both diffs directly to the working branch, conflicting line edits break the build. How should the orchestrator architecture resolve this?

options.text: Instruct all worker agents to push diffs directly to the repository working branch concurrently, letting git automatic merge resolution handle conflicts.
Configure workers to run at temperature zero so their generated diffs naturally align on the exact same line offsets without causing textual overlap.
Collect the candidate diffs at the orchestrator and execute an explicit synthesis and reconciliation step that integrates changes and verifies tests.
Discard the slower worker diff automatically and re-run that worker task serially against the committed modifications of the faster worker.

explanation: In the Orchestrator-Workers architecture, the orchestrator is responsible for both task delegation and synthesis. When concurrent workers produce complementary modifications to overlapping files, their outputs cannot be blindly concatenated or merged without coordination. The orchestrator (or a designated reconciler agent) must ingest both candidate solutions, synthesize a unified modification, and validate the combined change against test suites before committing.

distractorNotes.a: Concurrent uncoordinated git pushes cause merge conflicts, failed rebase operations, and broken builds when workers touch overlapping lines.
distractorNotes.b: Setting temperature to zero affects model sampling determinism within a prompt, but does not prevent two independently authored code changes from conflicting.
distractorNotes.d: Discarding valid work by the slower worker wastes tokens and latency, and re-running serially eliminates the throughput benefits of parallel delegation.

sourceNote: Orchestrator-workers: synthesis phase resolves worker conflicts and integrates results

stem: A developer productivity tool embeds Claude Code subagents to perform end-to-end integration test execution while an engineer interacts with the primary agent in a terminal session. The test suite takes four minutes to execute. If the primary agent runs the test tool synchronously, the interactive conversation locks up until the suite completes. Which architectural approach best maintains conversational responsiveness while managing test execution?

options.text: Execute the test runner synchronously within the main conversation turn while raising the client HTTP socket timeout to ten minutes.
Launch the test runner as an asynchronous background subagent and continue interactive dialogue, checking test status when notified.
Partition the four-minute test suite across twenty parallel synchronous tool calls invoked within a single conversational turn.
Instruct the model to simulate test execution outcomes in memory based on recent git diffs rather than invoking actual shell tools.

explanation: Claude Code and modern agent frameworks support asynchronous background subagents. When an operation requires extended execution time (such as compiling code or running a multi-minute test suite), running it as an asynchronous background agent allows the primary agent to return control to the user immediately. The primary agent can continue conversational interactions and inspect background agent status or receive completion notifications when the task finishes.

distractorNotes.a: Synchronous execution blocks the conversational session, freezing user interaction and leaving the client vulnerable to connection drops or perceived hangs.
distractorNotes.c: Invoking twenty parallel synchronous calls still blocks the turn until all calls complete, maintaining the conversational latency bottleneck.
distractorNotes.d: Simulating test execution hallucinates outcomes rather than executing real test suites against compiled binaries, masking actual regressions.

sourceNote: Async background subagents run long tasks without blocking the interactive primary agent session

stem: An autonomous accounts payable agent built with the Claude Agent SDK executes supplier payments using an in-process custom MCP tool (process_supplier_payment). During execution, an external payment API returns an HTTP 503 gateway error. To allow Claude to understand the specific transient failure and decide whether to retry or escalate without crashing the agent execution loop, how should the custom tool handler report this failure?

options.text: Throw an uncaught fatal exception from the tool handler function to abort the agent session immediately and prevent further tool execution.
Return a standard HTTP 200 mock response payload to Claude with an empty settlement identifier so the agent loop terminates cleanly.
Suppress the error silently inside the handler and return an empty string text block so Claude assumes the settlement succeeded.
Catch the failure and return a tool result with isError: true containing a composed error message explaining the 503 status and retry guidance.

explanation: In the Claude Agent SDK custom tool architecture, an error in a tool handler does not crash the agent loop. Catching the error and returning an object with `isError: true` (or `is_error: True` in Python) signals to Claude that the call failed rather than returning valid data, and allows the developer to compose an informative error message explaining the 503 status and suggesting next steps (such as retrying). Uncaught throws yield raw exception messages, while returning mock data or empty text misleads the model into believing the action succeeded.

distractorNotes.a: An uncaught throw in a custom tool handler surfaces a raw exception string to Claude rather than crashing the SDK process, but it deprives Claude of structured guidance on how to recover or retry.
distractorNotes.b: Returning mock success data misleads Claude into assuming the payment succeeded, which corrupts downstream accounting and prevents appropriate retry handling.
distractorNotes.c: Suppressing the error and returning an empty string hides the 503 failure from Claude, leading the model to hallucinate or report an unverified settlement.

sourceNote: Custom tool error handling: catch errors and return isError: true with a descriptive message for Claude to react without breaking the loop

stem: A cloud infrastructure migration agent built with the Claude Agent SDK executes a multi-hour database schema conversion spanning thirty sequential steps. During step 18, the ephemeral container hosting the worker process crashes due to an out-of-memory error and is rescheduled onto a new host. To ensure the agent can resume execution from step 18 without losing conversation history or re-executing completed steps, which architectural approach should the team implement?

options.text: Configure an external SessionStore adapter (implementing append and load) backed by a shared datastore, and resume the session by ID on the new host.
Set persistSession: false in the SDK client options so all state is maintained exclusively in process memory across container restarts.
Re-run the migration prompt from step 1 on the new container with a system prompt instructing Claude to skip any table that already exists.
Maintain session history in local container disk files under ~/.claude/projects/ and rely on ephemeral container volume mounts to survive rescheduling.

explanation: By default, the Claude Agent SDK writes session transcripts to local JSONL files under `~/.claude/projects/`, which do not survive container restarts or multi-host rescheduling. Implementing a `SessionStore` adapter with `append` and `load` methods allows the SDK to mirror session transcripts to an external datastore (such as an object store, key-value store, or database). When the worker container restarts on another host, passing the stored session ID to `resume` restores full conversation context and execution state.

distractorNotes.b: Setting persistSession: false keeps the session in memory only, which guarantees complete data loss when the container process terminates.
distractorNotes.c: Restarting from step 1 wastes tokens re-evaluating prior steps and risks partial state corruption or schema lock contention.
distractorNotes.d: Local filesystem paths under ~/.claude/projects/ are ephemeral to the specific container and do not survive rescheduling onto a different host.

sourceNote: SessionStore: implement append and load to mirror transcripts to external storage for durable resume across container restarts

stem: An automated refactoring agent built with the Claude Agent SDK modifies three core modules across two conversational turns using Edit and Write tools. An automated test suite run at turn 2 reveals severe type regressions. The orchestrator needs to revert all disk modifications made during turn 2 while preserving the conversation history so Claude can inspect the compiler errors and formulate a different refactoring approach. How does the Claude Agent SDK support this requirement?

options.text: Instruct Claude through a new user message to re-read each modified file and attempt to undo its recent string replacements in reverse order.
Terminate the session and execute git hard reset commands via the bash tool, since the SDK does not provide native file tracking or snapshot mechanisms across turns.
Call rewindFiles() with the checkpoint user message UUID, which restores modified files and deletes created files on disk while leaving context intact.
Call rewindFiles(), which rolls back both the files on disk and truncates all subsequent turns and compiler error messages from transcript memory.

explanation: The Claude Agent SDK provides file checkpointing, which automatically snapshots files modified or created via `Write`, `Edit`, or `NotebookEdit` tools at each turn, keyed by the user message's UUID. Calling `rewindFiles()` (or `rewind_files()` in Python) restores modified files to their checkpoint content and deletes newly created files on disk. Crucially, file checkpointing restores files on disk while leaving the conversation history and context intact, enabling Claude to reason over the previous attempt's failure output.

distractorNotes.a: Prompting the model to manually reverse its own edits is non-deterministic, error-prone, and consumes additional context tokens without restoring exact byte-level snapshots.
distractorNotes.b: The Claude Agent SDK includes native file checkpointing; relying on external git commands is unnecessary and risks wiping unstaged manual changes or repository metadata.
distractorNotes.d: File rewinding in the SDK restores files on disk to a previous state, but it explicitly does not rewind conversation history; transcript context remains fully intact.

sourceNote: File checkpointing: rewindFiles() restores files on disk to a checkpoint UUID while leaving conversation context intact

stem: An automated IT access management agent built with the Claude Agent SDK processes corporate role changes in non-interactive headless mode. Low-risk permissions are granted automatically, but elevated database access requires manual review and sign-off by a security administrator, which can take several business days. The architecture must suspend execution without keeping cloud compute instances idling or losing conversational context. Which TWO design practices allow the agent workflow to pause and resume durably? (Select TWO)

options.text: Keep the active container process running and execute a synchronous sleep loop that polls the ticketing system every five seconds.
Register a PreToolUse hook that returns permissionDecision: "defer" for privileged tool calls, ending the turn with stop_reason: "tool_deferred".
Hardcode administrator credentials into the agent system prompt so it can bypass manual sign-off when approval requests exceed four hours.
Resume the session by its session ID once human approval is granted, allowing the PreToolUse hook to return permissionDecision: "allow".
Discard the existing session entirely and spawn a fresh ungrounded agent instance that prompts the administrator to re-enter all employee details.

explanation: In non-interactive Claude Code and Agent SDK integrations, when a tool call requires human review or an out-of-band approval that will take longer than the session should wait, a `PreToolUse` hook can return `permissionDecision: "defer"`. This immediately pauses execution, ending the turn with `stop_reason: "tool_deferred"` and returning the session ID and deferred tool metadata without keeping compute instances running. Once approval is granted, the application resumes the session by ID; the `PreToolUse` hook fires again and returns `allow`, enabling execution to continue seamlessly.

distractorNotes.a: Long polling in an active container ties up compute resources, risks socket timeouts, and fails if the container restarts during the multi-day wait.
distractorNotes.c: Embedding administrator credentials in prompts circumvents security governance, creates severe vulnerability risks, and violates privilege separation.
distractorNotes.e: Discarding the session loses established context and validation history, creating friction and forcing repetitive manual data entry.

sourceNote: PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision: "defer" to pause with stop_reason: "tool_deferred", resuming later via session ID

stem: A financial regulatory filing engine must generate quarterly compliance disclosures following a mandatory five-stage procedure: data ingestion, threshold validation, variance auditing, legal review drafting, and executive sign-off formatting. In pilot testing with an autonomous agent given tools for all five stages, the model occasionally skipped variance auditing or executed sign-off formatting before legal review. Which architectural approach best guarantees strict procedural adherence?

options.text: Append emphatic instructions to the system prompt in capital letters commanding the agent never to deviate from the five-stage order.
Implement the process as a workflow where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths rather than an autonomous agent.
Run three autonomous agent instances concurrently and accept the filing only if at least two instances executed identical tool sequences.
Lower model sampling temperature to zero while adding ten synthetic few-shot demonstrations showing successful sequential tool runs.

explanation: Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' draws an architectural distinction between workflows and agents: 'Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths', offering predictability and consistency for well-defined, structured tasks. 'Agents, on the other hand, are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage.' For a mandatory, multi-stage compliance procedure requiring strict step sequencing, a workflow orchestrated through predefined code paths prevents the model from skipping or reordering steps.

distractorNotes.a: Prompt instructions provide soft behavioral steering rather than hard programmatic guarantees, and autonomous agents can still reorder or skip tools.
distractorNotes.c: Voting across three autonomous agents multiplies execution cost and latency by three without preventing failure modes shared across instances.
distractorNotes.d: Lowering temperature and adding few-shot examples improves pattern matching but does not provide deterministic code-path enforcement.

sourceNote: Workflows orchestrate LLMs and tools through predefined code paths for predictability, unlike agents which direct their own processes

stem: An engineering organization deploys four parallel worker agents to generate integration test suites across independent services in a shared repository. All workers execute concurrently in isolated workspaces. During execution, Worker 1 generates a shared mock authentication helper in tests/common/auth.py. Workers 2, 3, and 4 do not receive this update and each author incompatible, duplicate mock helpers in their respective workspaces. What state coordination mechanism best prevents this duplication?

options.text: Have the orchestrator maintain a centralized artifact registry and synchronization protocol to register and broadcast shared utilities.
Grant worker processes unconstrained concurrent write access to the same shared directory without locking or file synchronization controls.
Serialize all worker execution so that each test suite is generated strictly one after another over an extended sequential pipeline.
Instruct workers via system prompts to use bash grep commands to search other workers' private virtual machine filesystems every turn.

explanation: When parallel subagents operate across a shared problem domain, an out-of-band coordination mechanism is required to share common discoveries and artifacts. A centralized artifact registry or shared workspace synchronization protocol managed by the orchestrator allows workers to publish reusable components (such as shared mock utilities) and check for existing assets before authoring redundant, conflicting implementations.

distractorNotes.b: Unconstrained concurrent file writes without locking or coordination lead to file corruption, race conditions, and overwritten code changes.
distractorNotes.c: Complete serialization eliminates the throughput and latency benefits of parallel subagent execution when services are otherwise independent.
distractorNotes.d: Subagents operating in isolated execution environments cannot arbitrarily inspect private filesystems of sibling containers without established network shares.

sourceNote: Multi-agent coordination: orchestrators must provide synchronization mechanisms for shared artifacts

stem: An enterprise IT helpdesk system handles requests across four distinct categories: password resets, software license provisioning, network VPN diagnostics, and hardware replacement requests. A pilot implementation used a single monolithic agent with twenty tools covering all four categories. In production, the agent frequently selects incorrect tools, experiences high input token latency, and costs $0.12 per turn on simple password resets. Which architecture best resolves these operational issues?

options.text: Consolidate the twenty tool definitions into a single generic bash execution tool and let the model author bash scripts for all requests.
Invoke all four specialist category models in parallel on every user ticket and use a consensus voting mechanism to pick the best response.
Implement a classification router that directs user requests to lightweight, specialized handlers equipped only with category-specific tools.
Retain the monolithic agent prompt while increasing model thinking budget to maximum so the model evaluates all twenty tool schemas thoroughly.

explanation: The Routing pattern classifies incoming requests and dispatches them to specialized prompts, tools, or models optimized for that specific category. By routing simple password resets to a lightweight model with minimal tools, the system avoids loading twenty unnecessary tool schemas into context, eliminates tool selection ambiguity, dramatically reduces input token costs, and cuts response latency.

distractorNotes.a: A single generic bash tool increases security risk, removes structured schema validation, and worsens tool hallucination on simple administrative tasks.
distractorNotes.b: Running all four categories in parallel on every ticket quadruples inference costs and still requires downstream logic to discard irrelevant outputs.
distractorNotes.d: Maximizing thinking budget increases latency and cost on every turn without addressing tool schema clutter or context bloat.

sourceNote: Routing classifies inputs to direct them to specialized, scoped prompts and tools, cutting cost and confusion

stem: An engineering team is building automated verification pipelines for a financial clearing platform. Pipeline 1 must review pull requests across three distinct, orthogonal dimensions: security compliance, database migration safety, and API backward compatibility. Pipeline 2 must validate complex cryptographic signing algorithms where single model runs exhibit unpredictable stochastic oversights. Which TWO architectural pairings correctly map parallelization patterns to these requirements? (Select TWO)

options.text: Pipeline 1 should use Sectioning to evaluate security, database, and API dimensions concurrently with specialized prompts and aggregate findings.
Pipeline 1 should use Voting by running three identical general-purpose prompts and discarding any security finding not flagged by all three.
Pipeline 2 should use Sectioning by slicing the cryptographic algorithm into three isolated code snippets reviewed without cross-context.
Pipeline 2 should use Voting with diverse prompts or seeds across multiple runs to detect subtle vulnerabilities through pooled observations.
Both pipelines should be implemented as an autonomous unconstrained agent loop to let the model decide whether parallelization is required.

explanation: Anthropic's parallelization taxonomy distinguishes between Sectioning and Voting. Sectioning divides a task into independent, specialized subtasks executed concurrently (such as separate, focused reviews for security, database, and API compatibility) and aggregates their distinct outputs. Voting executes the same task multiple times with varied prompts, temperatures, or perspectives to achieve higher confidence or detect subtle edge-case bugs that a single run might miss.

distractorNotes.b: Voting across identical general prompts on Pipeline 1 would discard valid critical security findings if only one reviewer caught them, defeating specialized review.
distractorNotes.c: Slicing cryptographic code into isolated snippets destroys the cross-function algorithmic context needed to identify mathematical vulnerabilities.
distractorNotes.e: Unconstrained autonomous agent loops introduce serial latency, stochastic execution graphs, and unpredictable token costs without structural guarantees.

sourceNote: Parallelization: Sectioning breaks tasks into independent subtasks; Voting runs multiple passes on the same task for consensus

stem: A software team deploys an Evaluator-Optimizer loop to automatically modernize legacy code into idiomatic modern syntax. In initial testing, the generator and evaluator agents enter an infinite loop: the evaluator continuously suggests minor stylistic rearrangements (such as variable renames and comment rewording) without improving code functionality, burning through the token budget. Which architectural control best stabilizes this workflow?

options.text: Remove the evaluator agent and instruct the generator agent to evaluate its own code quality internally before emitting final tokens.
Define objective evaluation criteria with deterministic test execution and enforce a strict maximum iteration bound on the loop.
Raise the sampling temperature of the evaluator model to 1.0 to encourage more diverse and creative code critique suggestions.
Switch the evaluator agent to an autonomous agent loop with web search tools so it can search public forums for styling debates.

explanation: The Evaluator-Optimizer workflow is effective only when there are clear, measurable evaluation criteria and iterative refinement produces tangible value. Without objective stopping gates (such as deterministic test suites, linters, or a minimum quality threshold) and a strict hard ceiling on iteration count, the evaluator can offer perpetual subjective critiques that consume tokens without functional improvement.

distractorNotes.a: Self-evaluation within the generator suffers from self-reinforcing blind spots and lacks independent objective verification.
distractorNotes.c: Increasing evaluator temperature exacerbates subjective variability and inconsistency, increasing the likelihood of infinite loops.
distractorNotes.d: Adding web search tools introduces network latency and noise without establishing objective stopping criteria or iteration boundaries.

sourceNote: Evaluator-optimizer requires objective criteria, clear stopping conditions, and iteration bounds to prevent runaway loops

stem: A customer flight-booking assistant was deployed as an open-ended autonomous agent loop that sequentially searches flights, evaluates seat availability, queries hotel options, and prices rental cars. In production, 95th-percentile response latency exceeds 50 seconds and per-request costs escalate rapidly because the agent averages 16 serial tool turns, re-transmitting the accumulated conversation history on each turn. Which architectural refactoring best mitigates this latency and cost compounding?

options.text: Decompose the itinerary search into parallel subtasks executed concurrently via sectioning, then synthesize the results in a single step.
Retain the 16-turn serial agent loop but truncate tool schemas by removing argument descriptions to trim input token transmission.
Instruct the model via system prompt to skip intermediate flight validations and select the first available flight without tool verification.
Enable streaming output on all API calls so the client UI renders token chunks progressively while keeping the 16 serial steps unchanged.

explanation: Autonomous agent loops compound latency and cost linearly with turn count because each step requires a full network round-trip and accumulates token history (serial latency and quadratic input token growth without aggressive caching or clearing). For predictable composite tasks like travel booking, refactoring to parallel sectioning (searching flights, hotels, and cars concurrently) collapses the serial round-trips into a single parallel fan-out followed by a synthesis step, drastically slashing latency and cost.

distractorNotes.b: Trimming tool descriptions yields minor token reductions but fails to eliminate the primary bottleneck: 16 sequential model round-trips.
distractorNotes.c: Skipping validations causes inaccurate bookings, hallucinated flight numbers, and booking failures.
distractorNotes.d: Streaming improves time-to-first-token for individual calls but does not reduce total wall-clock duration or cumulative token cost across 16 sequential turns.

sourceNote: Agent loops compound latency and cost over deep turn counts; use parallel sectioning to collapse round-trips

stem: A customer support agent on the Messages API has prompt caching enabled to reduce costs across long conversations. The engineering team configures the application to inject dynamic per-request metadata—including the current UTC millisecond timestamp, a unique request identifier, and the active container ID—at the very beginning of the system prompt parameter on every turn. In production, metrics show that prompt cache read hit rates are 0%. What causes this issue?

options.text: The Messages API disables prompt caching automatically whenever conversations exceed five conversational turns.
Prompt caching requires that the system prompt be omitted entirely in favor of an initial user message containing instructions.
Modifying content at the start of the system prompt changes the prefix, invalidating the cached prompt prefix for all turns.
Cache breakpoints cannot be applied to system prompts and are valid only when placed on tool result blocks in user turns.

explanation: Prompt caching requires exact byte-for-byte prefix matching from the very beginning of the prompt. Placing dynamic, volatile values (such as timestamps, request UUIDs, or container IDs) at the start of the system prompt alters the initial tokens on every single turn, completely invalidating the cached prefix and preventing any cache read hits. To maintain cache prefix stability, static instructions and tools should be placed at the beginning, while dynamic or ephemeral metadata must be placed at the end of the prompt.

distractorNotes.a: The Messages API supports prompt caching across conversations of arbitrary turn lengths as long as token minimums are satisfied.
distractorNotes.b: Prompt caching fully supports the system prompt parameter; in fact, caching large static system prompts is a primary documented use case.
distractorNotes.d: Cache breakpoints (cache_control) are explicitly supported on system prompt blocks, tool definitions, and message blocks.

sourceNote: Prompt caching requires prefix stability: changes at the start of prompts invalidate the cache for all subsequent content

stem: A complex diagnostic agent assists engineers with database performance tuning over sessions that often reach 35 turns. To stay within the context window limit, the team configured a sliding window that retains only the 8 most recent conversation turns. Users report that after turn 12, the agent repeatedly asks for the database version and hardware specs that were provided in turn 1, and re-suggests indexing strategies that were already tested and rejected in turns 4 through 6. Which memory architecture best fixes this degradation?

options.text: Enlarge the sliding window buffer from 8 turns to 10 turns to capture earlier conversation turns without altering the truncation mechanism.
Implement structured summarization checkpoints that distill settled facts and ruled-out hypotheses into a persistent context block.
Prompt the user at turn 8 to paste their original database version and hardware specifications into the chat before proceeding further.
Eliminate conversation history entirely and convert each turn into a stateless single-turn prompt containing only the current user message.

explanation: Naive sliding-window truncation discards the oldest messages, which inevitably purges foundational constraints established at session intake (database version, hardware specs) as well as critical negative findings (tested and rejected indexing strategies). A structured compaction or checkpointing strategy addresses this by periodically distilling settled facts, operational constraints, and eliminated options into a persistent working memory block that survives window pruning.

distractorNotes.a: Slightly increasing the sliding window to 10 turns only delays the same failure mode until turn 14 without solving context loss.
distractorNotes.c: Relying on manual user re-entry degrades user experience and fails to preserve intermediate diagnostic findings discovered by the agent.
distractorNotes.d: Stateless single-turn prompting discards all prior context, exacerbating repetition and preventing iterative troubleshooting.

sourceNote: Context management: use structured compaction checkpoints to preserve critical early constraints and decisions

stem: An orchestration system fans out a code review task to 16 parallel subagents simultaneously. All 16 subagents share an identical 35,000-token system prompt containing coding standards, security rules, and architectural guidelines. The developers configure a cache breakpoint on the system prompt and issue all 16 API requests concurrently. Telemetry indicates that 15 of the 16 requests incurred full cache creation (write) token charges rather than cache read hits. Which TWO architectural adjustments ensure the parallel subagents benefit from prompt cache reads? (Select TWO)

options.text: Prepend a unique per-worker random identifier to the system prompt of each subagent to prevent concurrent cache read conflicts.
Issue a single warm-up priming request with the shared system prompt before fanning out the 16 parallel subagent review requests.
Delay the concurrent fan-out until the first subagent request has completed or begun streaming its initial response.
Remove the cache breakpoint from the system prompt and place it exclusively on the final line of each individual diff payload.
Reduce the size of the shared system prompt below 1,024 tokens so that the platform exempts the prompt from cache creation costs.

explanation: When using prompt caching, a cache entry is created and written during the execution of the initial request containing the breakpoint. If multiple requests with the same prefix are issued concurrently before the initial cache write has settled, each concurrent request encounters a cache miss and initiates its own independent cache write. To ensure parallel workers read from cache, the system must either issue a priming or warm-up request first or stagger the initial worker until its cache write completes before fanning out the remaining requests.

distractorNotes.a: Adding unique identifiers to each system prompt changes the prefix, guaranteeing 0% cache hits across all workers.
distractorNotes.d: Placing breakpoints on unique diff payloads fails because diffs differ per worker, preventing any shared prefix cache reuse.
distractorNotes.e: Prompts below 1,024 tokens are not cached at all; this eliminates caching rather than enabling cache reads.

sourceNote: Prompt caching: concurrent requests fired before a cache write finishes result in multiple writes; prime first

stem: A multi-turn architectural reasoning agent utilizes Claude's extended thinking capabilities to synthesize complex distributed system designs. Over an extended 18-turn session, accumulated thinking blocks from previous reasoning turns consume over 45,000 tokens of context, reducing the token capacity available for incoming tool results. The team wants to reclaim this context in ongoing turns without altering client-side message structures or losing Claude's visible text responses. Which built-in platform capability addresses this need?

options.text: Enable server-side thinking block clearing so the API automatically strips thinking blocks from prior turns in subsequent requests.
Set the thinking token budget to zero on subsequent turns, which instructs the model to delete historical thinking blocks from memory.
Configure client-side interceptors to strip user prompt turns while leaving all assistant thinking blocks intact in the message array.
Disable streaming response mode so that thinking blocks are omitted from the conversation history generated by the Messages API.

explanation: Claude's context editing features include server-side thinking block clearing. When enabled, the API automatically clears thinking blocks from earlier turns once that turn is complete, preserving the assistant's final text responses and tool interactions while freeing up tens of thousands of tokens of context for subsequent turns without requiring complex manual message manipulation on the client.

distractorNotes.b: Setting the thinking budget to zero disables extended thinking on the new turn; it does not clear thinking blocks already stored in conversation history.
distractorNotes.c: Stripping user prompts destroys conversational coherence and context while keeping the verbose thinking blocks that the team wanted to remove.
distractorNotes.d: Streaming mode controls how responses are delivered over the wire; it has no effect on whether thinking blocks are retained in conversation context.

sourceNote: Thinking block clearing automatically clears prior thinking blocks server-side to reclaim context capacity

stem: An internal operations agent on the Messages API aggregates tools from seven internal services and now exposes about 240 tools. The definitions alone consume roughly 60,000 input tokens per request before any work begins. Traces show Claude increasingly calling a near-duplicate tool from the wrong service, and the catalog keeps growing as teams onboard. Four tools appear in most sessions; the rest are used rarely. The agent depends on prompt caching of its tool and system prefix to keep long sessions affordable. Which change best addresses both the token overhead and the selection errors?

options.text: Have the application embed each user turn, pick the 15 closest tool definitions by similarity, and send just that subset in the tools array on each request.
Enable server-side compaction with a low trigger so the tool definitions are summarized together with older turns as the context nears its limit.
Mark every tool, including the four common ones and the search tool, with defer_loading so the starting context holds no tool definitions at all.
Add the tool search tool, defer loading of the rarely used tools while keeping the four common ones loaded, and still send the full catalog each request.

explanation: The tool search tool lets Claude discover and load tools on demand instead of holding every definition in context. Tool search typically cuts definition overhead by over 85 percent and keeps selection accuracy high, which otherwise degrades past 30–50 loaded tools. The API excludes deferred tools from the system-prompt prefix and appends each discovered tool inline as a tool_reference block, leaving the cached prefix intact. The documented practice is to keep the 3–5 most-used tools non-deferred, and every definition is still sent in the tools array because the API searches and expands them server-side.

distractorNotes.a: Plausible because it does shrink context, but the documented way to retrieve tools by embeddings is a custom search tool returning tool_reference blocks against a full deferred catalog. Swapping the tools array per turn changes the tool definitions at the front of the cached prefix whenever the subset changes.
distractorNotes.b: Compaction summarizes older conversation context; it does not reduce the number of tool definitions offered on each request, which drives both the per-request overhead and the documented drop in selection accuracy.
distractorNotes.c: At least one tool, normally the search tool itself, has to stay non-deferred, and a request with all tools deferred is rejected; the docs also recommend keeping the most frequently used tools loaded so Claude can call them without searching first.

sourceNote: Tool search: defer rarely used tools, keep 3–5 frequent ones loaded, send full catalog; tool_reference keeps the prefix cache

stem: A software-migration agent on the Messages API works on one repository across dozens of separate sessions over several weeks, and the team will move it to a newer Claude model partway through. Compaction keeps each session inside its context window, but each new session begins by re-exploring the codebase, and twice it re-implemented a feature an earlier session had abandoned after failed tests. The team wants every session to resume from where the previous one stopped. Which TWO design choices best achieve this? (Select TWO)

options.text: Enable the memory tool and rely on Anthropic to persist the /memories directory server-side between sessions, so no storage handler is needed in the app.
Prepend the previous session's full transcript to the first message of each new session so Claude sees every earlier decision and test result directly.
Add the memory tool with a handler that maps /memories onto a durable per-repository store, validates paths, and serves that store to later sessions.
Let Claude write memory notes ad hoc as it works and mark a feature done in its progress log once the code is written, keeping session overhead low.
Have an initializer session create a progress log and feature checklist, then open each session by reading them and close it by recording what was verified.

explanation: The memory tool lets Claude create, read and update files that persist between sessions, so it can record what it learns and read it back on demand rather than re-exploring. It is client-side: your handler maps the /memories prefix onto storage you control and must reject paths outside it. Because memory lives entirely in the application, a later conversation continues from it whenever it sends the same tools entry and the handler serves the same store. That continuity depends on the tools entry and the store rather than on the model, so it survives a model change. The documented multisession pattern adds structure: an initializer session sets up a progress log and feature checklist, each session reads them first and updates them before ending, and a feature is marked complete only after end-to-end verification. Compaction and memory are complementary: compaction keeps the active context small, and memory preserves what must survive summarization.

distractorNotes.a: The memory tool operates client-side: Claude only requests file operations, and your application runs each one against storage it controls. Nothing persists between sessions unless your handler stores it.
distractorNotes.b: Reloading whole transcripts loads everything up front, the opposite of the just-in-time retrieval memory supports, and long transcripts would overwhelm the context window that compaction is protecting.
distractorNotes.d: The documented pattern sets memory files up deliberately rather than ad hoc and marks a feature complete only after end-to-end verification, not when code is written; marking on write is how an abandoned feature gets recorded as done.

sourceNote: Memory tool: client-side store you control; multisession pattern with progress log and verified completion; pairs with compaction

stem: A release supervisor built on Claude Managed Agents delegates to two predefined subagents: a researcher with read-only GitHub MCP tools and a deployer whose MCP toolset includes a production deploy tool. To cut approval noise, the team set that toolset's permission policy to auto. Change-management policy requires a person to approve each production deploy. A post-incident review finds a deploy ran unreviewed after a support engineer's chat request, relayed into a user.message, asked for it. Which change best restores the required approval flow?

options.text: Keep auto on the deploy tool, since the server treats every deploy call as high-risk or indeterminate, and audit evaluated_permission on each event afterward.
Override the deploy tool's policy to always_ask, update the agent, start new sessions, and answer each paused deploy call with a user.tool_confirmation.
Reimplement deploy as a custom tool with an always_ask permission policy, so the approval request is raised by the application instead of the server.
Add a supervisor system prompt rule to confirm with a human before delegating any deployment, leaving the deployer's toolset policy as it is today.

explanation: Under auto, the server evaluates each call and runs it when it judges it safe, so auto is not a human checkpoint; the docs direct you to configure always_ask on any tool whose calls a person must review. A per-tool configs override sets always_ask on the deploy tool alone, and each deploy call then pauses the session until the client sends a user.tool_confirmation with allow or deny. Running sessions keep the toolset configuration they were created with, so the update applies only to sessions created afterward.

distractorNotes.a: Auto can allow a deploy outright, and relayed end-user text in user.message counts as intent that can get a call allowed. Auditing evaluated_permission afterward detects an unreviewed deploy rather than preventing it.
distractorNotes.c: Permission policies do not apply to custom tools; the application receives an agent.custom_tool_use event and decides for itself whether to run it, so an always_ask setting on a custom tool governs nothing.
distractorNotes.d: A prompt instruction is not an enforced checkpoint, and the deployer's own tool calls are still evaluated under auto; messages the supervisor sends a subagent do not change how those calls are permitted.

sourceNote: Permission policies: auto is not a human checkpoint; per-tool always_ask; custom tools exempt; running sessions keep config
